## Statement

Let $R:\Theta\times Z\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, where $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $Z\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ are open. Suppose $R(\theta_0,z_0)=0$ and the state Jacobian $R_z(\theta_0,z_0)$ is invertible. The Euclidean implicit function theorem gives a local $C^1$ solution branch $z=\phi(\theta)$, and
$$D\phi(\theta_0)=-R_z(\theta_0,z_0)^{-1}R_\theta(\theta_0,z_0).$$
For a scalar $C^1$ objective $J(\theta,z)$, its derivative along that branch is
$$D(J(\theta,\phi(\theta)))|_{\theta_0}=J_\theta-J_zR_z^{-1}R_\theta.$$
Equivalently, if $\lambda$ solves $R_z^T\lambda=J_z^T$, this derivative is $J_\theta-\lambda^TR_\theta$. These formulas concern the exact local solution branch; differentiating a stopped iteration is a separate finite-map derivative.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The residual equation, a $C^1$ residual, a square nonsingular state Jacobian, and a scalar $C^1$ objective.

[F1] [[thm-euclidean-implicit-function-theorem]]: for a $C^1$ Euclidean residual with zero value and invertible state-block derivative, there is a unique local $C^1$ solution branch and $D\phi=-R_z^{-1}R_\theta$.

[F2] [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: for $C^1$ maps $g,f$, $D(g\circ f)=Dg(f)Df$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** differentiate the exact solution identity.

1.1 Apply [F1] to $R$ with parameter block $\theta$ and state block $z$. It provides the local $C^1$ branch $\phi$ and the displayed formula $D\phi=-R_z^{-1}R_\theta$, under exactly the nonsingularity hypothesis in the statement. [F1, given]

2.1 The map $\theta\mapsto J(\theta,\phi(\theta))$ is $C^1$. By [F2], its derivative at $\theta_0$ is $J_\theta+J_zD\phi$. Substituting step 1.1 yields $J_\theta-J_zR_z^{-1}R_\theta$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Since $R_z$ is invertible, $R_z^T$ is invertible. The adjoint equation has the unique solution satisfying $\lambda^T=J_zR_z^{-1}$, by transposing $R_z^T\lambda=J_z^T$. Therefore $J_zR_z^{-1}R_\theta=\lambda^TR_\theta$, giving the stated adjoint formula. [given, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume exact arithmetic, a Hermitian positive-definite $A$, and a successful ordered factorization using [[alg-multifrontal-cholesky-and-sparse-triangular-solves]]. The fronts and contribution arrays give the same Cholesky factor as scalar elimination in ordering $\pi$. With $d_r=\ell_r+1=|F_r|$, the arithmetic work for assembly and scalar front updates is
$$O\!\left(\sum_{r=1}^n d_r^2\right),$$
the symbolic factor allocation has exactly $\sum_{r=1}^n d_r$ positions, and each forward/back substitution solve uses $O(\sum_r d_r)$ scalar operations. These are arithmetic and factor-storage counts; they are not wall-clock or total workspace bounds.

## Facts & Assumptions



**Given:** A Hermitian positive-definite matrix, an ordering, its filled graph and elimination forest, and exact-arithmetic multifrontal execution.

[F1] [[alg-multifrontal-cholesky-and-sparse-triangular-solves]]: Each nonzero off-diagonal entry and each diagonal entry is assigned once to its earliest endpoint's front; each front adds child contribution arrays, eliminates its one pivot by a Schur update, and retains every permitted symbolic factor slot.

[F2] [[lem-elimination-tree-reach-contains-each-filled-neighbor]]: For a child $s$ of $r$, $F_s\setminus\{v_s\}\subseteq F_r$.

[F3] [[lem-elimination-tree-reach-contains-each-filled-neighbor]]: Every later filled neighbor of a vertex lies on its parent path, so vertices in distinct descendant branches cannot have a filled edge.

[F4] [[thm-forward-and-back-substitution-are-correct-unique-and-quadratic-cost]]: Forward and backward substitution solve nonsingular triangular systems uniquely by the row recurrences stated in that theorem.

[F5] [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]: Every Hermitian positive-definite matrix has an exact Cholesky factor with positive diagonal, hence is nonsingular.

## Proof


1.1 For each vertex $v_r$, let $T_r$ be its subtree in the elimination forest and let $X_r=F_r\setminus\{v_r\}$. Define the local matrix for $T_r$ on $T_r\cup X_r$ to contain exactly the original entries assigned to fronts in $T_r$; its $X_r\times X_r$ block is zero, since entries wholly within $X_r$ are assigned to later fronts. If $u\in T_r$ and $w\notin T_r\cup X_r$ had an original edge, then either $w$ is earlier than $u$, making $u$ a later filled neighbor and ancestor of $w$, which would put $w$ in $T_r$, or $w$ is later than $u$, making $w$ a later filled neighbor and ancestor of $u$. In the latter case, repeated application of the child-column containment in [F2] from $u$ up to $v_r$ puts $w$ in $F_r$; since $w\ne v_r$ and $w\notin T_r$, it belongs to $X_r$. Both cases contradict the choice of $w$ by [F2,F3]. The induction invariant is that the returned array is the Schur contribution on $X_r$ after eliminating $T_r$ from this local matrix. If $v_r$ is a leaf, every entry assigned to its front has at least one endpoint $v_r$, so its initialized front is exactly this local matrix, with zero external-external block. The scalar update $C-bb^*/d$ therefore returns its Schur contribution. [given, F1, F2, F3, base, induction]

2.1 Let $v_r$ have children $v_{s_1},\ldots,v_{s_q}$. By [F2], each child interface $X_{s_h}$ lies in $F_r$, so every extend-add is defined. By [F3], there is no original matrix coupling between interiors of distinct child subtrees: such an edge would make its later endpoint a filled neighbor outside the earlier endpoint's parent path. Form the local matrix on the union of those child interiors and $F_r$, using only original entries assigned to these child subtrees or to $v_r$ and leaving entries wholly in $X_r$ zero. Its child-interior block is $D=\operatorname{diag}(D_1,\ldots,D_q)$, and its coupling to the current front is $B=[B_1\ \cdots\ B_q]$ partitioned by child subtree. Each $D_h=A[T_{s_h},T_{s_h}]$ is a principal submatrix of the positive-definite $A$, so it is positive definite; [F5] gives a Cholesky factor with positive diagonal and therefore shows $D_h$ is nonsingular. Its Schur complement on the current front is $C-BD^{-1}B^*=C-\sum_hB_hD_h^{-1}B_h^*$. The correction $-BD^{-1}B^*=-\sum_hB_hD_h^{-1}B_h^*$ is exactly the sum of child contributions by the induction invariant; adding them to the entries assigned to $v_r$ assembles this same local Schur complement. The pivot update $C-bb^*/d$ then eliminates $v_r$ and proves the invariant for $T_r$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, F5, IH, induction, algebra]

3.1 The invariant at each root eliminates all vertices. Each pivot column is therefore computed from the same exact Schur complement as scalar elimination in $\pi$, so the multifrontal factors equal the scalar Cholesky factors. [step 2.1, F1, algebra]

3.2 Front $r$ has $d_r=\ell_r+1$ indices. Its dense scalar pivot update and initialization from assigned entries use at most a constant multiple of $d_r^2$ arithmetic operations. Embedding and adding a child contribution touches at most that child's dense trailing block, whose entries are already counted by the child's $d_s^2$ bound. Summing over fronts gives $O(\sum_r d_r^2)$ arithmetic work. By [F1], each factor column retains one diagonal slot and all $\ell_r$ later-neighbor slots, including structural zeros, so symbolic factor storage is exactly $\sum_r d_r$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F2, algebra]

4.1 The forward column updates in [F1] solve $Lx=Pb$: after column $j$ is processed, row $j$ satisfies its equation, and the pivot contribution has been subtracted from each later row. This is the unique solution in [F4]. The descending conjugate updates solve $L^*y=x$ by the backward recurrence in [F4]. Since $PAP^*=LL^*$, these equations imply $PAP^*y=Pb$; multiplying by $P^*$ gives $A(P^*y)=b$. Thus $P^*y$ is the unique solution of $Az=b$. [step 3.1, F1, F4, algebra]

5.1 Each stored off-diagonal factor entry is visited once in each triangular solve, with one multiply and one subtraction; each diagonal contributes one division. Hence the two solves use $O(n+\sum_r\ell_r)=O(\sum_r d_r)$ operations, separate from the factorization work in step 3.2. [step 3.2, step 4.1, F1, algebra]

6.1 Step 3.1 gives scalar equivalence, step 3.2 gives factorization work and factor storage, and steps 4.1–5.1 give solve correctness and work. [step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 5.1, discharge-induction] ∎

## Definition

Input the original $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, the successful output record of [[alg-householder-bidiagonalization]] for $C=A$ if $m\ge n$ and $C=A^*$ otherwise, a deflation tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and a finite nonnegative integer sweep budget $N$. The reduction record supplies the upper bidiagonal work matrix $B_0$, dense accumulators $U_B,V_B$, and ordered stored local transformation data. Initialize $B=B_0$, the sweep accumulators $U_\Sigma,V_\Sigma$ to identities of order $p=\min(m,n)$, empty ordered left/right transformation lists, an empty deflation record, a pass counter $t=0$, and a sweep counter $s=0$. Write the diagonal as $d_i$ and superdiagonal as $e_i$, and set $e_0=0$.

At the start of each pass, set $t\leftarrow t+1$, set $e_i$ to zero and append $(t,i,e_i^{old})$ to the deflation record whenever $|e_i|\le\tau(|d_i|+|d_{i+1}|)$. The corresponding additive matrix change has entry $-e_i^{old}$ at $(i,i+1)$ and zero elsewhere. Record any later non-target sparsity cleanup the same way with its row, column, and old value. The zero entries split the active blocks. If every active block has size one, stop with `converged`. Otherwise process the active blocks in increasing order of $\ell$, skipping singleton blocks. Before each block sweep, if $s=N$, stop with `budget-exhausted`; otherwise form only the tridiagonal entries of $T=B^*B$ on that block: $T_{ii}=|d_i|^2+|e_{i-1}|^2$ and $T_{i,i+1}=\overline{d_i}e_i$. Choose $\mu$ to be the eigenvalue of the trailing Hermitian block $\begin{bmatrix}T_{r-1,r-1}&T_{r-1,r}\\T_{r,r-1}&T_{rr}\end{bmatrix}$ closest to $T_{rr}$, resolving a tie by the smaller eigenvalue. If the leading pivot $d_\ell$ is zero or has magnitude at most $\tau\max(|e_{\ell-1}|,|e_\ell|)$, use the zero-shift branch $\mu=0$ and choose the initial right Givens factor $G_\ell$ so that $(d_\ell,e_\ell)G_\ell=(\rho,0)$, avoiding division by the small or zero diagonal.

In the ordinary branch choose the first right Givens factor $G_\ell$ so that $G_\ell^*(T_{\ell\ell}-\mu,T_{\ell+1,\ell})^T=(\rho,0)^T$, where $T_{\ell+1,\ell}=\overline{e_\ell}d_\ell$. In either branch, apply $B\leftarrow BG_\ell$, update columns $\ell,\ell+1$ of $V_\Sigma$ by right multiplication by this same stored rotation, and append its exact unitary representative to the right list. For $j=\ell,\ldots,r-1$, choose a left Givens factor $H_j$ so that $H_j^*(B_{j,j},B_{j+1,j})^T=(\rho,0)^T$; apply it to rows $j,j+1$, update columns $j,j+1$ of $U_\Sigma$ by right multiplication by this same stored rotation, and append its exact unitary representative to the left list. On `budget-exhausted`, return the current $B$, accumulators, transformation lists, deflation record, triplet residuals, and orthogonality residuals. On `converged`, set $B_{\mathrm{final}}=B$ and return it with both dense accumulators, both transformation lists, the deflation record, triplet/orthogonality residuals, and its tall embedding $\overline B_{\mathrm{final}}=\begin{bmatrix}B_{\mathrm{final}}\\0_{M-p,p}\end{bmatrix}$.

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$ be Hermitian with strictly positive
diagonal, and let $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$. Write
$A=D-L-L^*$ by [[def-diagonal-lower-upper-splitting-convention]], and define

$$M_\omega=\omega^{-1}D-L,\qquad N_\omega=(\omega^{-1}-1)D+L^*,\qquad G_\omega=M_\omega^{-1}N_\omega.$$

The SOR iteration is $x^{(k+1)}=G_\omega x^{(k)}+M_\omega^{-1}b$. It converges
to the unique solution of $Ax=b$ for every $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb C^n$ if and
only if $A$ is positive definite (meaning $x^*Ax>0$ for every nonzero $x$)
and $0<\omega<2$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n\ge1$, a Hermitian matrix $A$ with positive diagonal, a real
$\omega\ne0$, and arbitrary $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb C^n$.

[A1] $A=A^*$, $a_{ii}>0$, and $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$.

[F1] SOR uses $M_\omega=\omega^{-1}D-L$ and
$N_\omega=(\omega^{-1}-1)D+L^*$
([[alg-sor-stationary-iteration]]).

[L1] The fixed diagonal/lower/upper convention gives $A=D-L-L^*$ for
Hermitian $A$ ([[def-diagonal-lower-upper-splitting-convention]]).

[L2] For an invertible matrix $M$ and $A=M-N$, the stationary update is
$x^{(k+1)}=M^{-1}Nx^{(k)}+M^{-1}b$
([[def-stationary-iteration-from-a-matrix-splitting]]).

[L3] This iteration converges to the unique solution for every right-hand
side and every start exactly when $\rho(M^{-1}N)<1$
([[thm-stationary-splitting-converges-iff-the-iteration-matrix-has-spectral-radius-below-one]]).

[L4] Hermitian positive definite means $A=A^*$ and $x^*Ax>0$ for every
nonzero $x$ ([[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]]).

[L5] A lower-triangular system with nonzero diagonal has a unique forward
substitution solution ([[thm-forward-and-back-substitution-are-correct-unique-and-quadratic-cost]]).

[L6] Determinants are multiplicative for same-sized square matrices over a
commutative ring ([[thm-determinant-multiplicative]]).

[L7] The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal
entries ([[thm-determinant-of-a-triangular-matrix]]).

[L8] When the characteristic polynomial splits as $\prod_i(t-\lambda_i)$,
the determinant is $\prod_i\lambda_i$
([[thm-determinant-is-product-of-eigenvalues]]).

[L9] Every complex polynomial splits over $\mathbb C$
([[thm-the-complex-numbers-are-algebraically-closed]]).

## Proof


1.1 By [A1] and [F1], $M_\omega$ is lower triangular with diagonal $a_{ii}/\omega\ne0$, hence invertible by [L5]. Also $A=M_\omega-N_\omega$ by [L1], so [L2] applies with iteration matrix $G_\omega$. The matrix $N_\omega$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $(\omega^{-1}-1)a_{ii}$. Thus [L6]–[L7] give $\det(M_\omega)=\omega^{-n}\prod_i a_{ii}$ and $\det(N_\omega)=(\omega^{-1}-1)^n\prod_i a_{ii}$. From $M_\omega G_\omega=N_\omega$ and multiplicativity, $\det(G_\omega)=\det(N_\omega)/\det(M_\omega)=(1-\omega)^n$. [A1, F1, L1, L2, L5, L6, L7, algebra]

1.2 For sufficiency, suppose $A$ is positive definite and $0<\omega<2$. Then $Q:=M_\omega+M_\omega^*-A=(2/\omega-1)D$ is positive definite. For an eigenpair $G_\omega v=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, one has $\lambda\ne1$ since $Av=(1-\lambda)M_\omega v$ and $A$ is invertible. Put $a=v^*Av>0$. Then $v^*M_\omega v=a/(1-\lambda)$, so $v^*Qv=a\left(2\operatorname{Re}\frac{1}{1-\lambda}-1\right) =a\frac{1-|\lambda|^2}{|1-\lambda|^2}>0$. Therefore $|\lambda|<1$ for every eigenvalue and $\rho(G_\omega)<1$. [A1, F1, L1, L2, L4, algebra]

2.1 If SOR converges for every right-hand side and start, [L3] gives $\rho(G_\omega)<1$. By [L8]–[L9], $|\det(G_\omega)|=\prod_{j=1}^n|\lambda_j|\le\rho(G_\omega)^n<1$. Step 1.1 therefore gives $|1-\omega|<1$, which for real $\omega$ is equivalent to $0<\omega<2$. [L3, L8, L9, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Assume now that SOR converges for every right-hand side and start. Then $\rho(G_\omega)<1$ by [L3], so $1$ is not an eigenvalue of $G_\omega$ and $I-G_\omega$ is invertible. By [L2], $A=M_\omega(I-G_\omega)$ is invertible. For $b=0$, its unique solution is $x_*=0$. For arbitrary $e^{(0)}:=x^{(0)}$, set $e^{(k)}:=x^{(k)}-x_*=x^{(k)}$ and $\delta_k=e^{(k+1)}-e^{(k)}$. The homogeneous SOR recurrence gives $M_\omega e^{(k+1)}=N_\omega e^{(k)}$, hence $Ae^{(k)}+M_\omega\delta_k=0$. Expanding the Hermitian quadratic form gives $(e^{(k)})^*Ae^{(k)}-(e^{(k+1)})^*Ae^{(k+1)} =\delta_k^*(M_\omega+M_\omega^*-A)\delta_k =(2/\omega-1)\delta_k^*D\delta_k$. The last equality follows from [L1] and [F1]. [A1, F1, L1, L2, L3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By step 2.1, $c:=2/\omega-1>0$. Summing the identity in step 2.2 from $k=0$ to $N-1$ and taking $N\to\infty$ (the error tends to $0$ by the assumed convergence) gives $(e^{(0)})^*Ae^{(0)}=c\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta_k^*D\delta_k$. Moreover $\delta_0\ne0$: otherwise step 2.2 implies $Ae^{(0)}=0$, contrary to invertibility of $A$. Since $D$ has positive diagonal, the first summand is strictly positive and all others are nonnegative. Thus $(e^{(0)})^*Ae^{(0)}>0$ for every nonzero $e^{(0)}$, so [L4] gives that $A$ is positive definite. [A1, L3, L4, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 By [L3], $\rho(G_\omega)<1$ implies convergence to the unique solution for every right-hand side and every initial vector. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the reverse implication. [L3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Remarks

The conclusion is exact-arithmetic asymptotic convergence; it is not a
one-step error decrease or a finite-precision accuracy guarantee. No
optimal-$\omega$ formula is asserted.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a
bounded polyhedral open set with a matching shape-regular affine simplicial
mesh family $\{\mathcal T_h\}$, and set $h:=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}h_K\le1$.
Fix an integer $r\ge1$. On the reference simplex let
$(\widehat S_d,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ be an unisolvent real scalar
finite element whose finite-dimensional local space $\widehat P$ consists of
polynomials and contains $\mathbb P_r$. Assume each
degree of freedom has a bounded linear extension to
$W^{r+1,2}(\widehat S_d)$, and let $\widehat I$ be its interpolant. Suppose
there is a global map $I_h$ whose restriction to each cell is the affine
pullback of $\widehat I$, and that $I_hu\in V_h$ for the conforming discrete
space $V_h\subset H^1_0(\Omega)$ whenever
$u\in W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)\cap H^1_0(\Omega)$, where $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is the
closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ in $W^{1,2}(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). Then a constant $C$ independent of
$h$ and $u$ satisfies
$$\|u-I_hu\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C h^r|u|_{W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
The global conformity and zero-boundary mapping property of $I_h$ are explicit
hypotheses; this estimate does not assert them for arbitrary degrees of
freedom.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice; the exact matching affine mesh convention; a reference element with $\mathbb P_r\subseteq\widehat P$ and bounded degrees of freedom on $W^{r+1,2}$; the cellwise affine interpolation formula; and the stated global mapping property $I_hu\in V_h$.

[F1] An unisolvent reference element has a unique linear interpolation operator that reproduces every polynomial in its finite-element space ([[def-reference-finite-element-and-unisolvent-dofs]], [[lem-unisolvent-dofs-define-reference-interpolant]]).

[F2] On the reference simplex, for real-valued $w\in W^{r+1,2}$ there is $q\in\mathbb P_r$ with $\|w-q\|_{W^{m,2}}\le C|w|_{W^{r+1,2}}$ for $m=0,1$ ([[thm-bramble-hilbert-on-reference-simplex]]).

[F3] Affine pullback and pushforward transform order-$m$ Sobolev seminorms by the corresponding powers of $A$ and $A^{-1}$ and determinant factors ([[lem-affine-pullback-weak-derivatives-and-scaling]]).

[F4] Shape regularity gives $\|A_K\|\le Ch_K$, $\|A_K^{-1}\|\le Ch_K^{-1}$, and $\det A_K\asymp h_K^d$ ([[lem-shape-regular-affine-simplex-scaling]]).

[F5] Countable Choice is assumed by the Sobolev and affine-change suppliers used in [F2]–[F4] and by the Lebesgue measure suppliers in [F6] ([[def-countable-choice]]).

[F6] Lebesgue outer measure is defined by elementary-set covers; half-open boxes have their product volume, and every outer-null set is measurable and null ([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]]).

## Proof

1.1 On the reference cell write $\widehat Iw=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(w)\widehat\phi_i$. Each degree of freedom is bounded on $W^{r+1,2}$ by **Given**, and each fixed polynomial shape function has finite $W^{1,2}$ norm. Thus $\|\widehat Iw\|_{W^{1,2}}\le C\|w\|_{W^{r+1,2}}$. By [F1], $\widehat Iq=q$ for every $q\in\mathbb P_r$. For such $q$, $w-\widehat Iw=(w-q)-\widehat I(w-q),$ so $\|w-\widehat Iw\|_{W^{m,2}} \le\|w-q\|_{W^{m,2}}+C\|w-q\|_{W^{r+1,2}}\qquad(m=0,1).$ [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Choose the polynomial $q\in\mathbb P_r$ supplied by [F2]. Since $m\le1\le r+1$, [F2] bounds both terms in step 1.1 by $C|w|_{W^{r+1,2}}$. Hence the reference-cell interpolation error obeys $\|w-\widehat Iw\|_{W^{m,2}}\le C|w|_{W^{r+1,2}}$ for $m=0,1$. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 For a cell $K$ with affine matrix $A_K$, apply [F3] to transform the reference error and the order-$(r+1)$ derivative seminorm back to $K$. The determinant factors cancel; the remaining factor is bounded by $C\|A_K^{-1}\|^m\|A_K\|^{r+1}\le C h_K^{r+1-m}$ by [F4]. Therefore $\|u-I_Ku\|_{L^2(K)}\le C h_K^{r+1}|u|_{W^{r+1,2}(K)},\qquad |u-I_Ku|_{W^{1,2}(K)}\le C h_K^r|u|_{W^{r+1,2}(K)}.$ [F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $E_h:=\bigcup_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\partial K$, a finite union of simplex facets. Each facet lies in a bounded affine hyperplane; choose a coordinate with nonzero normal component and write that hyperplane as the graph of an affine function over a bounded box in $\mathbb R^{d-1}$. Partition the base box into at most $C_0N^{d-1}$ boxes of side $1/N$. The affine function varies by at most $C_1/N$ on each, so each graph piece lies in a slightly enlarged half-open $d$-box of volume at most $C_2N^{-d}$. These elementary-set cover members have total volume at most $C_0C_2/N$; the outer-measure definition and box-volume formula give outer measure zero for the facet, and completeness makes it Lebesgue-null. Thus $E_h$ is null, and $\Omega\setminus E_h$ is the disjoint union of the cell interiors by the mesh definition. Square and sum the estimates in step 3.1 over these interiors; the sums of squared Sobolev seminorms equal the corresponding global seminorms. Since $h_K\le h\le1$, the order-zero contribution $h_K^{r+1}$ is at most $h^r$. The global interpolation map in **Given** takes values in $V_h$, yielding $\|u-I_hu\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C h^r|u|_{W^{r+1,2}(\Omega)}$. [given, F4, F5, F6, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, let $f\in C^2(U,\mathbb R)$ have an attained global minimum $f^*=f(x^*)$ at $x^*\in U$, and fix $x_0\in U$. Suppose $K:=\{y\in U:f(y)\le f(x_0)\}$ is compact and is contained in a convex open $V\subseteq U$ that contains every Newton backtracking trial segment under consideration. For constants $0<m\le M$, assume

$$m\|v\|_2^2\le v^TH_f(y)v\le M\|v\|_2^2\qquad(y\in V,\ v\in\mathbb R^d).$$

Assume also that there are $R>0$ and $L_H\ge0$ with $B(x^*,R)\subseteq V$ and $\|H_f(y)-H_f(z)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L_H\|y-z\|_2$ for $y,z\in B(x^*,R)$, where $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$. Let $\rho>0$ and $C<\infty$ be constants furnished by [[thm-newton-local-quadratic-convergence-under-lipschitz-hessian]] for these data, and set

$$\tau_N:=\min\left\{1,\frac{2b(1-a)m}{M}\right\},\qquad q_N:=1-\frac{2am\tau_N}{M}.$$

For every accepted update before entry into $B(x^*,\rho)$,

$$f(x_{k+1})-f^*\le q_N(f(x_k)-f^*),\qquad 0<q_N<1.$$

Thus, after finitely many such updates the method either has stopped at its positive decrement test or has entered $B(x^*,\rho)$. More explicitly, if $\varepsilon<m^2\rho^2/(2M)$, the decrement test cannot stop outside that ball, so the method reaches it after finitely many accepted updates. Once in this ball, every later attempted update has step $t_k=1$ and satisfies

$$\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|_2\le C\|x_k-x^*\|_2^2.$$

The last assertion is conditional on the decrement test not stopping first. No post-stop iterate or update is asserted. This is a strongly convex objective result; it does not apply to arbitrary vector roots or indefinite Hessians.

**Given:** The hypotheses of the Statement, a generated iterate $x\in K$, and the canonical damped-Newton line-search parameters and decrement test.

[F1] [[alg-damped-newton]]: when $H_f(x)$ is positive definite it computes $p=-H_f(x)^{-1}\nabla f(x)$ and $\lambda^2=\nabla f(x)^TH_f(x)^{-1}\nabla f(x)$; if $\lambda^2/2\le\varepsilon$ it stops before line search, and otherwise it backtracks from $t=1$ using the Armijo condition with parameter $a$ and factor $b$.

[F2] [[thm-newton-local-quadratic-convergence-under-lipschitz-hessian]]: for a $C^2$ objective with a positive-definite critical Hessian and a Lipschitz Hessian on a ball, every generated iterate from a sufficiently small ball remains there; each attempted update whose decrement test does not stop has unit step and a quadratic error bound.

[F3] [[lem-hessian-lower-bound-strong-convexity-gradient-gap]]: the Hessian lower bound gives $f(x)-f^*\ge m\|x-x^*\|_2^2/2$ and $\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\ge2m(f(x)-f^*)$.

[F4] [[thm-multivariable-taylor-formula-with-lagrange-remainder]]: on a segment in the convex domain, the second-order remainder is a Hessian quadratic form at an interior point.

[F5] [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]: a real symmetric Hessian has an orthonormal eigenbasis, so $mI\preceq H\preceq MI$ implies $M^{-1}I\preceq H^{-1}\preceq m^{-1}I$.

[F6] [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]] and [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]: the Hessian of a $C^2$ real scalar objective is symmetric and uses the second-partial convention.

[F7] [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]: $\nabla f$ is the vector of first partial derivatives.
